lesson.title: Gaining Electrons: How Atoms Become Negatively Charged
lesson.summary: Anion formation is the process by which atoms gain one or more electrons to become negatively charged ions, usually releasing energy in the process and completing the electron transfer that ionic bonding depends on.
lesson.body:
An anion is an atom, or group of atoms, that has gained one or more extra electrons and therefore carries a net negative charge. Unlike cation formation, which always costs energy, adding an electron to a neutral atom is often energetically favorable, releasing energy rather than consuming it. The energy change when a gaseous atom gains one electron is called electron affinity, and for most nonmetals, that first electron affinity is exothermic, meaning energy is given off as the new electron settles into an available orbital and is drawn toward the nucleus.

Chlorine is a clean example. Chlorine's electron configuration is one electron short of a filled argon-like shell, so adding a single electron to its 3p subshell is strongly favorable, releasing about 349 kilojoules per mole and producing Cl-, with the electron configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6, identical to argon. This is the same logic that runs through cation formation in reverse: atoms move toward the nearest noble gas configuration, whether that means losing electrons to reach the previous noble gas or gaining electrons to reach the next one.

Oxygen shows why the story does not always stop after one electron. Oxygen's first electron affinity is exothermic and favorable, adding one electron to give O-. But oxygen commonly forms the 2- ion, O2-, not the 1- ion, and adding that second electron is actually unfavorable on its own. An electron approaching an already negatively charged O- ion is being pushed away by electrostatic repulsion, so the second electron affinity step requires an energy input rather than releasing one. Oxygen still ends up as O2- in real compounds like magnesium oxide because the energy cost of that second step is more than repaid once O2- pairs up with a cation and the resulting lattice energy is released, the same kind of energy bookkeeping introduced when lattice energy was defined.

The elements that form anions most readily sit on the right side of the periodic table, especially the halogens in group 17, which need only one electron to complete an octet, and the chalcogens in group 16, like oxygen and sulfur, which need two. Metals almost never form anions, because their valence electrons are held so loosely that adding more electrons to an already electron-poor arrangement is not favorable, which is exactly why cation formation belongs to metals and anion formation belongs to nonmetals.

Anion formation only tells half of the ionic bonding story. A chlorine atom gaining an electron to become Cl- has no chemical reason to do so in isolation, since removing that electron again would just cost the energy back. What makes the whole process worthwhile is pairing that anion with a cation, such as Na+, so that the resulting electrostatic attraction, the ionic bond, releases far more energy than either the ionization step or the electron affinity step consumed on its own, ultimately building the same kind of stable, high lattice energy crystal seen in sodium chloride.
